title: the banner saga
text: Words do not describe the pure emotion and beauty this game instills. It is slow paced at times, but it works for its method of story-telling and its overall feel. Every choice you make has weight in the world and for the characters living in it, sometimes to beautiful or even devastating effects. A few things have been left unexplained, which leads me to believe a sequel would be planned. Dear god I hope so. I have never before felt so strongly about a game as a work of art and storytelling that must be experienced. In summary, if you believe in games as a medium of art, then I cannot recommend any game more highly than The Banner Saga.

title: the banner saga
text: After a discrete experience as a videogamer I learned to classify games into macro-categories, more or less like steam tags. But there are some games, some little pearls, that lie outside every class. If you open the store page of The Banner Saga, it'll tell you that the game is a turn based RPG. Don't believe it. The tag is a lie. That is such a reductive definition that is like to say that the Hamlet is just a tragedy. The Banner Saga redefines itself presenting a game experience that does perfectly what a game should do: it carries you into another world, makes you feel what the characters feel, to the point I wasn't able not to finish it in one day. In the short, but at the same time long days of marching followed by your caravan, you feel the weight of leadership, the eyes of every person weighting your decisions, the fear of hunger for every day you pass in the open, with the supplies running short, the relief of entering a village and rest. Regarding the combat system, it may not be very innovative, but it wasn't meant for casual players, that's sure. On normal difficulty, enemies will smash you and leave you wounded for days, even after victory, if you don't put strategy and caution in your decisions. To cut it short, just because you are giant wielding a battle axe that doesn't mean that rush into enemies swinging it is a good idea. I suggest everyone to play this game. If you want more than entertainment from a game, if you want to feel something, if you want to fear, joy and cry (I admit it, just a little in the end), give it a try. "Why are we alive, when even the gods are dead?"

text: This is one of the more refreshing RPGs I have played...and in a while too. It's testament that a good game does not need advanced graphics and effects to make the player have a good time. Anyway...I can't really find anything negative to say about The Banner Saga, although at the end I was left wanting for more. It is short in my opinion and it could use some more features, like bigger battles and more RPG elements such as conversations. I for one hope to see more of this in the future!

text: To be honest, I was kind of disappointed with banner saga. The begining looked wonderful, and the art style is beyond my expectations. That being said, you eventually have to play the game. The game is like Oregon trail, where you lose supplies/people because you didn't guess the right prompt.  The story is told though dialog boxes which severely disappointed me considering the opening annimation was awesome. Then the rest was just a guy standing there in a picture with a dialog box; he doesn't move his mouth or motion, just a portriat of him. Then entire game. Combat has.... some..... stratagy to it. Armor and strength. You wittle away armor and try to take away as much strength as you can before the enemy does. In same cases, the AI doesn't play statigically and just hits the closest thing to it. In some cases they focus one target until it is dead. increasing the difficultly only adds more AI with this midset. Of course, you play the same tactic, only to realize each hero can only level up by last hitting the enemy. So yea, some stratagy. Some spoilers beyond this point but was my biggest gripe with the game. The story is cut half way through the game, leaving alot of room for a sequel. Though, trying to justify the price of $25 for a story that is cut just at the good part made me feel more conned then hoping for a sequel. Kind of like Halo 2 "Sir, to finish this fight" CREDITS!

title: the basement collection
text: I have been a fan of Edmund Mcmillen ever since he was back on Newgrounds, so the second I saw a compilation of all of those games redone come on sale, I was quite excited to jump back into the fray of the physics-platformers the man is known for, especially the original Meat Boy, which is fairly nostalgic to me. Now, briefly, let me sum up the games: they're fine. They're still well designed, sometimes brilliant little games that achieve so much with so little. I enjoy Spewer's, Time ♥♥♥♥'s, Aether's new smoother, crispier selves. Meat Boy was thrown under the bus. Meat Boy is a very good game with consistent controls. These controls, while a tad floaty, are suited to the game's design. Meat Boy jumps just within the right height and width the character needs to see to the end of the level, turning this struggle into an elegant foray of taps and clicks. Every time you press the space bar, you feel in control of the hang time and brevity of the leap. It's simple and comfortable for a game with vertically designed levels in mind. Super Meat Boy's levels are, for the most part, horizontal, and designed for a controller. So, whoever decided to throw out the original controls in turn for these new ones is an idiot. Meat Boy, as a game where it's levels are designed with the controls in mind, does NOT work with new controls. Simple. Now the game plays like an awkward, floppy piece of meat, where instead of dancing across levels, now feels as entertaining as swinging a stick around in a figure 8. Also, the stick is falling apart, constantly. As SOON as you let go of the space button, Meat Boy plummets to the ground as fast as he left. There is no arch like there was in the original, just because more people played Super Meat Boy and that's what they're used to. And hey, on a controller, I'M used to that too! But guess what? No controller support! AND, you can't change the controls back to the original! MAN. I LIKE THIS REDESIGN.

title: the basement collection
text: Edmund McMillen is a professional troll and game designer with a perverted and vile sense of humor. He's also a genius. He's the man behind the modern classics Super Meat Boy and The Binding of Isaac, titles you should already recognize if you've been a Steam gamer for any amount of time. The Basement Collection is a compilation of his old flash games which made him famous on Newgrounds. Granted, it's an excellent compilation, complete with tons of extra levels and DVD extras, but whether it's worth your time or not really just boils down to the question "How eager are you to play these games again?" I say this, because this collection mainly exists for historical significance alone. The games themselves are low-res, glitchy, have mildly-to-maddeningly infuriating controls, and most of them are simply exercises in masochism. They’re the type of game you beat just to be able to say you beat it, and that it’s finally over with. In other words, a good challenge. But if you want to unlock all the extras that make this package worth the money, you’ve got to play through the games again. So it all comes down to how appealing that sounds to you. If these games are important to you and mean something to you, if they were the games that defined your childhood and the games you'd secretly play in computer lab in high school or something, hey, I respect that. Buy it without hesitation and support the man who gave you hours of joy in your youth. We all have our nostalgia bombs and we have every right to indulge. But if you've never played these games before, there are much better Edmund McMillen games on the market, as well as better games to play for their historical significance alone; I recommend seeking those out instead. (Oh, and it’s also quite hard to 100%, so achievement hunters beware!)

text: Run. While you still can. This game is worse than WoW. I can't stop playing it. I hate it, but then why am I still playing it? I'll tell you why. It toys with you. It lulls you into a false sense of security with trinkets that enchant you with their beguiling colors. As you survive further and further with each dive into the abyss, you unlock even more items. These empower you with strange abilities that allow you to challenge bosses at the end of each floor. These festering kings guard the way out, but this is a trick.  Each horror after misshapen horror toppled from thrones of baby skulls only brings you that much closer to your inevitable fate as you delve deeper into the "basement." Eventually, sin will overwhelm you as you start gambling with your ill-gotten wealth. You start spending hours playing the slots in the arcade. As you lust for power, count on making poorly informed decisions, defended blindly with protests of "how was I supposed to know the treasure room contained only a measly glass of chocolate milk?" or "One more coin. Just one more coin and I'll get that soul heart." Ultimately, all the time and effort you put into your playthrough, dozens of near-death experiences and blood sacrifices will flash before your eyes when you are slain by a fly. Then, the whole process starts all over again. Do you dare to try where others have failed? Do you dare to buy this game? Don't like stories? Then take this list as I bleed out on my keyboard.

title: the bridge
text: I really liked this game a lot, but then I've always loved the drawings of MC Escher. A deep, considered, puzzle game. Not good if you're looking for quick action, not a great deal of story or character development (though there is some), but the puzzles really require some consideration, a bit of trial and error, and later on particularly a deep understanding of the mechanics that are progressively introduced. It's the kind of puzzle game that would drive a lot of people to looking up instructions for solutions I think, or others still to try 100 times then sleep on it and suddenly have the answer. A lot of people have drawn comparisons with Braid, which I haven't played, but I really felt this was more inspired by Escher's original drawings than any other game and similarities in mechanics were not intentional. Others still have stated the controls are clunky or slow, which I also disagreed with. I played on PC, with keyboard only (no controller). The pace of the game is slow, but this fits well with the style and atmosphere and the nature of the puzzles. The character moves slowly, but this gives you quite fine control over where he's standing and how he's sliding around when you shift gravity, which becomes critical to solving many of the later puzzles.

title: the bridge
text: The Bridge is an homage to the art of M.C. Escher. If you don't know who that it is, it doesn't really matter as the game stands alone well enough. The puzzles are complex enough to be challenging at times but not in a cerebral manner. More often than not I knew what I was supposed to do to finish the puzzle, I simply had difficulty doing it because it required a precise maneuver. This became very frustrating to me at times as on some of the levels I ended up getting smashed by the little lion marble things over and over again simply because I couldn't fall or move precisely right. Having also played games like Antichamber, Portal and Portal 2, I found this games puzzles to be much more annoying than the puzzles which those games present (which wasn't a good thing) as the puzzles of those games didn't rely so much on that precision. In many ways, the game is essentially a digital version of this little marble game I played as a kid. The game consisted of a marble which you had to guide (by titling the board) through a maze rife with holes. If your marble fell into one of the holes as you were tilting the board, you had to start over. The game was never a riddle as you knew you had to tilt the board to get by the holes, but it was difficult because of the skill required to move the marble precisely how you wanted. The Bridge is basically an updated version of this. The game does boast a fairly unique build and look and the artwork at times is intriguing. There is little to no storyline however and what little they do incorporate is very esoteric. The game does feature an interesting soundtrack, but it is underutilized. The gameplay was interesting enough to me to finish it (which took less than ten hours) and so I think I can recommend it if you can purchase it while the game is on sale. If it's not, you may not feel like you're getting your money's worth and you probably shouldn't buy it. If, in the end, you are an enthusiast of Escher's artwork and impossible figures and structures (such as endless staircases etc) then it may be worth the full price of the game, but otherwise just wait for the price to drop.
